e.meaning: short form of Yahweh, the Hebrew name of God
e.etymology: From Hebrew Yah, the short form of the divine name, as in hallelujah, praise Jah. It is the usual name of God in Rastafari and the first syllable of names such as Jahmir and Jahleel.

assoc.t: Jah, the name of God in Rastafari and reggae

e.etymology: A respelling of Maisie, a Scottish pet form of Mairead, the Gaelic form of Margaret. Margaret comes from Greek margarites, pearl.
The Ukrainian form of Salome, from the Hebrew root of shalom, peace. The soprano Solomiya Krushelnytska is its best-known bearer in Ukraine.
Nova, Latin for new and the word for a star that suddenly brightens, joined with the -lyn ending.
A short form of Wilhelmina, the feminine of Wilhelm (William), from Germanic wil, will or desire, and helm, helmet or protection.
namesakes: Wilma Flintstone (The Flintstones)
Wilma Rudolph (Olympic sprint champion)
Wilma Mankiller (first woman chief of the Cherokee Nation)

assoc.t: Hurricane Wilma, which struck Florida in 2005

e.meaning: from the Roman clan name Claudius
e.etymology: The French form of Claudius, the name of a Roman clan, in English use since the 16th century. It is traditionally tied to Latin claudus, lame, though the clan name is more likely Sabine.
namesakes: Claude Monet (Impressionist painter)
Claude Debussy (French composer)

e.etymology: A respelling of Ashley, an English place name and surname from Old English aesc, ash tree, and leah, clearing.
namesakes: Ashlee Simpson (pop singer)

e.etymology: A pet form of Amanda, from Latin amanda, worthy of love. It has also been used as a full name since the mid-20th century.
namesakes: Mandy Moore (singer and This Is Us actress)
Mandy Patinkin (actor in The Princess Bride and Homeland)

e.etymology: From the Scottish surname and clan name Leslie, taken from a place in Aberdeenshire whose Gaelic name is read as garden of hollies. Lesley is the traditional British spelling for girls.
namesakes: Lesley Stahl (60 Minutes correspondent)
Lesley Gore (singer of It's My Party)

e.etymology: From Latin Hilarius and its feminine Hilaria, from hilaris, cheerful. Saint Hilary of Poitiers made it a man's name in the Middle Ages; it has been mostly feminine since the 20th century.
namesakes: Hilary Swank (Oscar-winning actress)
Hilary Duff (actress and singer)
Hilary Banks (The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air)

assoc.t: actresses Hilary Duff and Hilary Swank
Hillary Clinton, by sound (she spells it with two l's)

e.etymology: A German short form of names containing the Germanic element frid, peace, such as Friederike and Elfriede.
The feminine form of Leander, from Greek Leandros, from leon, lion, and aner, man. In Greek legend Leander swam the Hellespont each night to reach Hero.
An African American coinage of the 1970s that sets the La- prefix on the ending of Terrell.
namesakes: Latrell Sprewell (NBA All-Star guard)

e.etymology: From Spanish azucena, the white Madonna lily, a word taken from Arabic. The flower is a symbol of the Virgin Mary.
From Arabic anwar, more luminous, the comparative of the word for bright, built on nur, light.
namesakes: Anwar Sadat (Egyptian president and Nobel Peace laureate)

e.etymology: A feminine spelling of Perry, an English surname for someone who lived by a pear tree. Use for girls peaked after Disney's 1957 film Perri, about a young squirrel.
The Italian form of Peter, from Latin Petrus and Greek Petros, rock, the name Jesus gave to the apostle Simon.
namesakes: Pietro Maximoff (Quicksilver in Marvel comics and films)

e.etymology: An African American coinage that joins the Ty- of Tyrone and Tyrell to the sound of Tariq. Tyrik, Tyrique and Tyreke are other spellings.
namesakes: Tyreek Hill (NFL wide receiver)

e.etymology: An English place name and surname from Old English draeg, a drag or portage, and tun, settlement: a place where logs or boats were hauled.
The German, Dutch, Czech and Russian form of Edward, which reached the Continent through French Edouard. Edward is Old English ead, wealth, and weard, guardian.
A spelling of Jaycee, which began as the initials J.C. written out and is also used as a pet form of Jay and Jacey.
A Spanish surname from romero, a pilgrim, originally one who travelled to Rome. Romero is also the Spanish word for rosemary.
namesakes: George A. Romero (director of Night of the Living Dead)
Cesar Romero (actor who played the Joker in 1960s Batman)
Oscar Romero (Salvadoran archbishop and Catholic saint)

e.etymology: A spelling of Yaneli, a modern name used mainly in Mexican and Mexican American families. Its source is not established.
A spelling of Rania, an Arabic name from the verb rana, to gaze at. The best-known bearer is Queen Rania of Jordan.
An English surname meaning son of Tenney, a medieval form of Dennis. As a first name it honors the Victorian poet Alfred, Lord Tennyson.
A short form of Alexa or Alexandra, from Greek alexein, to defend, and aner, man. It rose in the 2010s with the character Lexa in the TV series The 100.

assoc.t: Commander Lexa of the CW series The 100

e.meaning: pet form of Adelaide, Adeline or Addison
e.etymology: A pet form of names beginning Ad-: chiefly Adelaide and Adeline, from Germanic adal, noble, and Addison, son of Adam.
e.note: Addy is also casual slang for an address and for the ADHD drug Adderall.

assoc.t: Addy Walker, American Girl's Civil War-era doll
addy, slang for Adderall, and for an address

e.etymology: The German and Scandinavian form of Amalia, from Germanic names beginning with amal, vigor or bravery. Amelia is the English relative. Amalie has been a royal name in Denmark.
The English word jewels used as a name. It also works as a phonetic spelling of Jules, the short form of Julia and Julian.

assoc.t: jewels, the everyday word for gems and jewelry

e.meaning: heaven, a place of perfect happiness
e.etymology: The English word, from Greek paradeisos, a park or garden, itself borrowed from an Old Iranian word for a walled enclosure. It names the Garden of Eden and heaven.
